questions.title: What level of harm is required to constitute "persecution" under the INA, and why don't threats alone qualify?
questions.question_body: I'm reading the Tenth Circuit's decision in Jimenez v. Bondi where the court held that repeated threats at gunpoint, combined with psychological harm, did not constitute past persecution. The court says threats alone are insufficient and that the harm must be "more than just restrictions or threats to life and liberty." But the applicants were held at gunpoint and told they would be killed. The court also mentions they consider incidents collectively under the cumulative effects doctrine. How much harm is actually required? Does physical injury have to occur? What makes threats cross the line into persecution?

questions.title: How does the "mixed-motive" analysis work for establishing nexus in asylum cases?
questions.question_body: The court in Jimenez found that the persecutors had multiple motives - Jimenez's professional involvement in the property dispute AND his political opinion. The court said the political opinion was "tangential and subordinate" to the main reason (threatening Don Rafa's revenue and security). The opinion cites that a protected ground must be "at least one central reason" for persecution, not just a minor role. I'm confused about how courts determine which motive is "central" when persecutors mention multiple reasons during the threats. Here, the gunmen called them "snitches for the police" and mentioned they were "in politics" - so why wasn't political opinion considered central?

questions.title: What constitutes evidence that a government is "unable or unwilling" to protect asylum applicants?
questions.question_body: The court held that Petitioners failed to show the Colombian government was unable or unwilling to protect them. The opinion emphasizes that they only spoke to two individual police officers and didn't report to higher authorities, even though Jimenez had law enforcement connections through his work. The court says "a one-off conversation with an unhelpful officer" doesn't prove government inability. But the officer told them nothing could be done and that police were "contributing to the problem." How much evidence of government complicity or failure is actually required? Does an applicant need to exhaust all reporting options before proving futility?

questions.title: How does the "substantial evidence" standard of review constrain appellate courts in asylum cases?
questions.question_body: The opinion repeatedly states that the BIA's findings are "conclusive unless the record demonstrates that any reasonable adjudicator would be compelled to conclude to the contrary." This seems like an extremely deferential standard. The court says it's not their prerogative to "reweigh the evidence." I'm struggling to understand when an appellate court can actually reverse BIA factual findings under this standard. Is this essentially a rubber-stamp review? What would have to be in the record for the court to find the evidence "compels" a contrary conclusion?

questions.title: What is the relationship between asylum and withholding of removal standards?
questions.question_body: At the end of the opinion, the court states that "because Petitioners fail to demonstrate a well-founded fear of persecution under asylum standards, they necessarily fail to meet the higher standard for withholding of removal." I know withholding of removal has a "more likely than not" standard compared to asylum's "well-founded fear" standard. But are there other differences? And can someone qualify for withholding even if they don't qualify for asylum, or are the requirements essentially the same except for the burden of proof?

questions.title: When can an applicant successfully argue that internal relocation within their home country is not reasonable?
questions.question_body: The court found that Petitioners could safely relocate within Colombia because they stayed with Jimenez's mother in the countryside for three weeks unharmed, and the threats specifically told them to leave their "neighborhood" not the country. Petitioners argued relocation was unworkable due to administrative burdens and their persecutors' ties to the president. The court dismissed these as "hypothetical hardships." What factors actually make internal relocation unreasonable? Does the persecutor's geographic reach matter, or is it purely about whether the applicant personally can find safety somewhere in the country?

questions.title: Can past political activity that predates the actual persecution establish nexus to a protected ground?
questions.question_body: The court noted that before Jimenez's confrontation with Don Rafa, the family received threats related to their Liberal Party membership and continued campaigning despite a colleague being murdered. But the court found the escalated threats came only after the property dispute. Does prior political persecution that's unrelated to the main persecutor count for establishing nexus? The court said there was no evidence Don Rafa was behind the initial political threats - so if a different group persecuted someone politically first, does that help establish that later persecution by someone else was also politically motivated?
